inputs.need:
I am the stroke neurologist at a 400-bed regional hospital that is the primary stroke centre for a mostly rural catchment. We thrombolysed 94 patients last year. Our median door-to-needle time was 62 minutes, and only 27 percent of patients were treated within 45 minutes, which is our network's target. Every case is timed, so we know where we stand, but we do not really know where the minutes go.

We plan a quality improvement project: first map the process from ambulance pre-alert to needle with everyone involved (paramedics, emergency nurses, the CT radiographer, the stroke team and pharmacy), and then test changes in PDSA cycles over six months. Ideas people have raised include taking the patient straight to CT on the ambulance stretcher, preparing the thrombolytic while the scan is running, having the stroke nurse meet the ambulance at the door, and a single group page instead of three separate calls. Night and weekend cases seem slower because the stroke registrar comes in from home.

I need help with the aim statement, the right outcome, process and balancing measures (for example symptomatic haemorrhage and treatment of stroke mimics), how to show monthly data when we only treat seven or eight patients a month, and how to run the mapping so that nobody feels blamed. We cannot hire anyone, and the CT scanner is shared with the emergency department's trauma cases.
inputs.constraints: No new staff or funding. Six-month project from January to June 2027. The CT scanner is shared with trauma, so changes must not delay trauma imaging.

records.title: Direct-to-CT transfer on the ambulance stretcher and door-to-needle times at a regional stroke centre: an improvement report
records.authors: Oduya-Hartmann L, Pike-Mensah R, Solberg-Achebe T
records.abstract: At a regional stroke centre treating about 100 patients a year with thrombolysis, direct transfer to CT on the ambulance stretcher and pre-notification reduced median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes over 18 months. The proportion treated within 45 minutes rose from 31 to 69 percent. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 5 percent of treated patients before and 4 percent after the change. Treatment of stroke mimics rose from 2 to 5 percent. Night and weekend cases improved less than weekday daytime cases, and the authors describe the out-of-hours pathway as the next target.

records.title: Process mapping of acute stroke thrombolysis pathways: where do the minutes go?
records.authors: Castellanos-Nyberg A, Obi-Fairweather K, Haddad-Lund M
records.abstract: In four hospitals, observers timed 160 thrombolysis cases step by step. The largest delays occurred between arrival and CT (median 17 minutes) and between CT and the treatment decision (median 14 minutes). Drug preparation added a median of 7 minutes when it started after the decision. Delays were longest when the stroke physician was not present at arrival. Hospitals that paged the whole team with one call had shorter arrival-to-CT times than hospitals that called team members one by one.

records.title: Door-to-needle times at night and weekends: an analysis of a regional stroke dataset
records.abstract: Using a regional stroke dataset of 3,420 thrombolysis cases, median door-to-needle time was 12 minutes longer at night and at weekends than in weekday daytime. The difference was largest in hospitals where the stroke registrar was on call from home. Out-of-hours patients were not more severely affected on arrival. Hospitals that had moved to a single group page for the stroke team showed a smaller out-of-hours gap. The analysis could not separate the effect of staffing from the availability of imaging and radiographers, which also fell out of hours in most hospitals.

records.title: Balancing measures in stroke thrombolysis improvement: haemorrhage and stroke mimics
records.abstract: We reviewed 22 improvement reports that shortened door-to-needle times. Twelve reported symptomatic haemorrhage and nine reported treatment of stroke mimics. Symptomatic haemorrhage did not rise in any report, while treated mimics rose in four reports, reaching 6 percent in one. Most reports had too few patients to detect a change in haemorrhage. We recommend reporting both measures with their numerators and denominators, not only rates, and reviewing every treated mimic. Reports that reviewed every treated mimic described most as migraine, seizure or functional presentations with a benign course.

records.title: Statistical process control with small monthly samples: run charts for door-to-needle times
records.authors: Varga-Okonkwo H, Reid-Castellano B, Sato-Lindgren E
records.abstract: Stroke centres treating fewer than ten patients a month produce unstable monthly medians. Using simulation and data from 30 hospitals, we show that case-by-case run charts of individual door-to-needle times, with a median line and the standard run rules, detect a sustained 15-minute improvement within about 20 cases, whereas monthly medians need five to six months. An individuals chart can flag unusually long cases for review without waiting for a monthly summary. The authors provide a template and advise freezing the baseline median before any change is tested.

records.title: Team debriefs after every thrombolysis case: feasibility and time to treatment
records.abstract: In two hospitals, the treating team held a two-minute debrief after each thrombolysis case, recording the main delay on a card. Debriefs were held after 81 percent of cases. Staff described them as blame-free when a nurse led them. Median door-to-needle time fell by 9 minutes over six months, alongside other changes. Recorded delays most often concerned CT availability and paging. Night teams held debriefs less often than day teams. The authors could not separate the effect of debriefs from the other changes made at the same time.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; four model leads remain unverified and are not appraised. Direct-to-CT transfer with pre-notification cut median door-to-needle time from 58 to 36 minutes at a comparable regional centre, and time studies place most delay between arrival and CT and between CT and the decision, with late drug preparation and serial paging adding minutes. Out-of-hours cases are 12 minutes slower where the registrar is on call from home. Treated mimics can rise with faster pathways, so they and haemorrhage are balancing measures. Case-by-case run charts suit a centre treating seven or eight patients a month.
response.gradeRationale: Improvement reports and observational time studies, mostly single-centre and uncontrolled; consistent direction for pathway changes, low certainty about effect size here.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low; leads left unverified.

steps.note: Appraisal of the six retrieved records only (S13); the leads are untouched and stay unverified. Certainty is assigned over the inspected records (G1).

response.reading: The minutes are spent in two stretches: from arrival to CT, where the patient waits for triage, a trolley and the scanner, and from CT to the decision and drug, where the team assembles and the drug is prepared after the decision. Serial paging and the registrar's travel lengthen both, most at night. The retrieved reports show that direct-to-CT, a single group page and preparing the drug during the scan remove these waits, at the cost of more treated mimics if the pace outruns assessment. Trauma imaging competes for the same scanner.

response.overview: Six-month QI project using the Model for Improvement: two mapping sessions in December 2026, then PDSA cycles from January to June 2027, with every thrombolysis case plotted on a run chart against the 2025 to 2026 baseline.

response.designSummary: Run chart of individual door-to-needle times, with the 2025 to 2026 baseline median as the centre line and standard run rules; an individuals chart to flag unusually long cases.
response.sampleSize: About 94 cases a year give roughly 45 to 50 cases in six months. With case-by-case plotting, a sustained 15-minute improvement is expected to trigger the shift rule within about 20 cases (c5), so a real change should be visible by the third cycle. The baseline uses the last 12 months of cases (about 94), which gives a stable median. Balancing measures are too rare for statistical comparison and are reviewed case by case.

response.title: Shortening door-to-needle time at a regional primary stroke centre through process mapping and PDSA cycles
response.abstract: Problem: median door-to-needle time of 62 minutes with 27 percent treated within 45 minutes. Intervention: mapping with all staff involved and four PDSA cycles (direct to CT, single group page, drug preparation during CT, out-of-hours extension) with nurse-led debriefs. Measures: door-to-needle time per case on a run chart; haemorrhage, treated mimics and trauma delays as balancing measures. Results will be written after June 2027.
response.introduction: Faster thrombolysis improves recovery after ischaemic stroke. Time studies place most delay between arrival and CT and between CT and the treatment decision, and small centres struggle to see change in monthly figures.
response.methods: The Model for Improvement guided two mapping sessions and four PDSA cycles from January to June 2027. Every case was plotted on a run chart with rules fixed before cycle 1, and the project was screened as quality improvement.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will show the run chart of every case with cycle dates marked, the step-time charts and the balancing measures with numerators and denominators.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate chart signals to the cycles and consider out-of-hours cases separately. It will review every treated mimic and haemorrhage against the speed gained.
response.limitations: This is a single centre with about 50 cases, and balancing measures are too rare to compare statistically. Secular changes in the regional network may contribute.
response.conclusion: To be written after the final cycle. It will report whether the aim was met and which changes the centre will keep.
